chapter: Chapter I — An Old-School Gentleman Gone Mad

facts: Once upon a time there lived in a village in Spain, in the province of La Mancha, one of those gentlemen of the old school
He keeps an ancient lance and shield hung up in his hall, and maintains a riding horse and a hunting dog
About three-fourths of his income went in household expenses
The remainder kept him in decent clothes: a best suit for Sundays and holidays, and one of good homespun for everyday use

glossary.homespun: Loosely woven fabric, usually wool or linen, made from yarn spun at home.

facts: His household consisted of an elderly housekeeper, a niece of his under twenty, and a handyman who could help in the house or outdoors
Our gentleman was about fifty, thin, but tough of body, with a lean face, a very early riser, and a great lover of hunting
His name was Quixania
He got into the habit of reading romances of chivalry with such ardor and intensity that at last he lost interest in hunting and even neglected his daily concerns
He sold several acres of good cropland in order to buy as many books about chivalry as he could lay his hands on
He passed whole days and nights studying the preposterous adventures of Don Belianis, Amadis of Gaul and other knights
At last his brain became so agitated and his judgment so warped that he resolved to become a knight himself and ride about the world setting wrongs right and seeking adventures
The first thing he did was polish up some old armor that had belonged to his ancestors and had lain for ages in a corner, covered with dust and rust

glossary.chivalry: The ideals of medieval knights that emphasized gallantry, honor and courtesy, especially toward women. The stories of knights whose adventures illustrated the spirit of chivalry were called romances.

facts: Picture caption: The first thing he did was polish up some old armor
He found he had one great deficiency: there was no helmet, only a simple steel cap
By means of some cardboard he made a visor that, fixed to the cap, gave the appearance of being a complete helmet
He got the idea to test its strength for resisting cuts, and drawing his sword he made a stroke at it and in one instant demolished it
The work he destroyed had taken a whole week
Deciding to make something stronger, he got strips of iron and made them a lining to the cardboard
He then declared his new visor sufficiently strong, without risking any more experiments on it
His horse had as many points as a mariner's compass and was only skin and bone, but appeared to him a charger superior to the Bucephalus of Alexander
He spent four days considering what he should name the horse
After making up and rejecting many possible names, he at last fixed on Rocinante

glossary.Bucephalus of Alexander: Legendary for his speed and courage, Bucephalus was the favorite horse of Alexander the Great. After he died of battle wounds at the old age of 30, Alexander founded a city named for him in what is now Pakistan.

facts: To his thinking Rocinante was a lofty and resonant name, signifying that the horse that before had been a mere hack was now the foremost of all the hacks in the world
He thought about a name for himself for eight days more and at last decided in favor of Don Quixote
Remembering that the valiant Amadis added the name of his country, Don Quixote enlarged his name to Don Quixote de la Mancha
Thereby he judged he made clear his origin and honored his country by adopting its name
A knight-errant without a lady-love was like a tree without leaves or fruit, or a body without a soul
He imagined sending a vanquished giant, Caraculiambro, to present himself before his lady

glossary.hack: A horse hired out for any use and generally worn out from hard work.

facts: In his own neighborhood there was a very good-looking farmer's daughter whom he had once been smitten with, though she did not seem to know or care anything about him
Her name was Aldonza Lorenzo and he thought her fit to be the lady of his heart
He called her Dulcinea del Toboso, since she was a native of Toboso, a name that seemed to him musical and significant
One morning before daybreak, on one of the hottest days in July, he donned his armor, mounted Rocinante, stole away through a private gate of his yard and reached open country
His joy was short-lived: he suddenly remembered he had not been dubbed a knight in the proper form
According to the laws of chivalry he had no right to wear anything but white armor, nor to carry a device on his shield, until he had earned one through his exploits
So great was his concern at this discovery that he almost turned back, but his folly overcame every other impulse and he continued on
He resolved to get himself knighted by the first knight he should come across
As to the white armor, he would scour his own so that it would be whiter than ermine
He allowed his horse to follow whatever road it pleased, considering this to be the true spirit of adventure
They jogged along all day, Don Quixote suffering enough intense heat from the sun to melt his brains, if he had any
Night approached without any adventure, and both horse and rider were quite worn out and almost dead from hunger
He began to look for a castle, or a shepherd's hut, where he could find food and rest
At last he saw an inn not far from the road and reached it just before nightfall
By the door there stood a couple of young wenches

glossary.white armor: A young man about to be made a knight first confessed all his past deeds and then put on a white tunic to symbolize his purity on entering into the order of chivalry. The ceremony conferring knighthood had similarities to the Christian ritual of baptism.
glossary.device: The design or emblem a knight chose that identified him, often his family crest.

facts: The two girls were on their way to Seville and stopping for the night at the inn
Everything he thought, saw or imagined was tinted and transformed by the nonsense he gathered from his books of chivalry
He at once pictured this inn as a castle with four towers, spires of polished silver, a drawbridge and moat, and all the usual features of castles in romances
He waited for a dwarf or page to announce his arrival by the blast of a trumpet from the battlements
Rocinante was impatient to get to the stable, so he advanced nearer the door
He caught sight of the two girls, who appeared to him to be two beautiful damsels
A pig-driver blew on his horn to call his herd from a nearby field, and at once Don Quixote recognized this as the signal of his arrival
He approached the ladies, who were alarmed at the sight of a man so strangely outfitted and bearing a lance and shield

glossary.Seville: The chief city of southern Spain. Long held by the Moors, it was a center of learning and the capital of bullfighting.
glossary.page: A youth in training for knighthood who is a personal servant to a knight.

facts: Don Quixote gracefully raised his cardboard visor, revealing his lean, dusty face, and addressed the girls in soothing tones
He told them not to fly and not to be uneasy, since it would ill become a member of the order of chivalry to do wrong to anyone
The girls were astonished and amused at being addressed in this fashion
The landlord, a fat, good-natured fellow, came out to receive his odd-looking guest, helped him down and attended to his wants and those of Rocinante
In the course of conversation the landlord readily made out the kind of madness from which the stranger suffered

The host knew a great deal about the romances of knights-errant and could not resist the chance to play along with the folly of Don Quixote in order to amuse himself and his guests, who were mostly passing herdsmen and mule drivers
As soon as Don Quixote had satisfied his hunger he approached the innkeeper, fell on his knees and begged him in very flowery language to dub him a knight
The innkeeper graciously agreed, but reminded Don Quixote that he must first pass a night watching his armor
Picture caption: Don Quixote begged him in very flowery language to dub him a knight
Don Quixote asked to be taken to the chapel to lay his armor in front of the altar
The host explained that the chapel had recently been demolished so that it might be rebuilt, and suggested that the ceremony take place in the courtyard
Such a thing might be done in cases of necessity, he said, as was recorded in the histories of famous knights
So Don Quixote removed his armor and put it in a trough in one of the yards of the inn
For hours he marched up and down in front of the trough, lance in hand, in the bright moonlight, to the amusement of the landlord and his friends
As the night wore on, one of the mule drivers came into the yard to fetch water for his mules and laid hands on the armor in order to move it
The vigilant Don Quixote gave him such a thwack on the head with his lance that he was knocked out
A second mule driver, on the same errand, approached the trough and began handling the armor, and promptly met the same fate as the first
The comrades of the injured men rushed into the yard in anger and began pelting the knight with anything they could pick up
Don Quixote bravely stood his ground, sheltering himself with his shield and hurling defiance and threats back
The landlord arrived, fearing he was responsible for letting the joke go too far, and anxiously called on the drivers to stop their attack
He reminded them that they were dealing with a madman who would not be held accountable for his actions, even if he killed some of them
In this way the tumult came to an end, and the landlord next considered how he could speedily get rid of his dangerous guest
A full-page illustration by Gustave Dore

The picture shows Don Quixote standing alone with his lance, watching his armor by moonlight, with his armor on the wall beside him
